title: AP U.S. Government and Politics Independent Foundation Pilot
description: An independently authored 260-question AP U.S. Government and Politics foundation pilot spanning all five current units and all 60 current public framework topic IDs. Every topic has at least three practice angles, including a transfer/application layer, with a thirteen-document foundational-document crosswalk, expanded constitutional, institutional, source, data, argumentation, and item-linked study-route coverage for internal QA and study-route testing.
disclaimer: Independent, unofficial AP U.S. Government and Politics preparation material for internal foundation-pilot development only. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or authored by College Board. This pilot does not provide official scores, score predictions, college-credit predictions, or a substitute for civics instruction.
contentReview: Two hundred sixty original, source-aligned draft multiple-choice items: all five current units and all sixty current public framework topics are represented at least three times, with all five course skill categories and twenty-three named subskills sampled. Each of the fifteen native lesson sections carries a linked foundation/depth/transfer study route and topic-level drill map; a thirteen-document public foundational-document list is crosswalked by title and topic with deterministic item, section, and workshop study routes without reproducing document text; and the learning library adds five explicitly unscored response-planning workshops. This is an internal foundation, not an official exam form or calibrated readiness measure.

items.prompt: A community creates a government by agreeing to surrender some freedom in exchange for protection and public order. Which democratic ideal is illustrated?
choices: The social contract
Popular sovereignty
Judicial review
Federalism
items.rationale: The social contract describes an implicit agreement in which people accept some limits so government can provide order and protection.
choiceRationales: The social contract describes an implicit agreement in which people accept some limits so government can provide order and protection.
Popular sovereignty says authority comes from the people, but the scenario describes the exchange of some freedom for protection, which is the social contract.
Judicial review is a court power to strike down unconstitutional acts; it has nothing to do with why people form a government.
Federalism divides power between national and state governments; the scenario is about the origin of government itself, not its levels.

Judicial supremacy

items.prompt: Which claim best represents the Federalist argument that a large republic could protect liberty?
choices: A large republic eliminates all political factions by requiring unanimous agreement among representatives.
A large republic makes state governments unnecessary because local interests disappear as territory expands.
A large republic can make it harder for one faction to dominate by multiplying interests and representatives.
A large republic protects liberty only when voters are barred from replacing the officials who represent them.
items.rationale: Federalist No. 10 argued that an extended republic could control faction by making majority combinations more difficult and by filtering public views through representation.
choiceRationales: Madison argued factions cannot be eliminated without destroying liberty; the goal is to control their effects, not to require unanimity.
Federalist No. 10 did not propose abolishing states; it argued more interests across a larger territory make any one faction less likely to dominate.
Federalist No. 10 argued that an extended republic could control faction by making majority combinations more difficult and by filtering public views through representation.
The argument relies on elections filtering public views through representatives, so removable officials are part of the design, not a threat to it.

items.prompt: Why did Shays’ Rebellion strengthen arguments for revising the Articles of Confederation?
choices: It demonstrated that the national government had an overly powerful executive.
It proved that Congress could directly regulate interstate commerce.
It showed that the national courts could easily enforce federal law.
It exposed national weakness in responding to internal unrest.
items.rationale: The rebellion exposed weaknesses in the Confederation government, including its limited military and fiscal capacity, and encouraged support for a stronger national framework.
choiceRationales: The Articles created no separate national executive at all, so the rebellion could not expose an executive that was too strong.

Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress had no authority to regulate interstate commerce; Shays’ Rebellion instead underscored the national government’s inability to raise troops or funds to quell domestic uprisings.
There was no national court system under the Articles; enforcement depended on the states, which is why the unrest alarmed nationalists.
The rebellion exposed weaknesses in the Confederation government, including its limited military and fiscal capacity, and encouraged support for a stronger national framework.

items.prompt: What was the principal effect of the Great Compromise at the Constitutional Convention?
choices: It paired population-based House seats with equal state representation in the Senate.
It gave every state an identical number of representatives in both chambers regardless of its population.
It replaced congressional representation with direct national voting by citizens on every proposed law.
It required the president to be selected by the Supreme Court rather than by electors chosen in the states.
items.rationale: The Great Compromise balanced large-state and small-state interests by combining proportional representation in the House with equal state representation in the Senate.
choiceRationales: The Great Compromise balanced large-state and small-state interests by combining proportional representation in the House with equal state representation in the Senate.
Equal representation applies only to the Senate; the House is apportioned by population, which was the compromise itself.

The Constitution established a representative republic rather than direct national democracy, so the Great Compromise structured a bicameral Congress instead of allowing citizens to vote directly on every federal statute.
Presidential selection runs through the Electoral College; the Court plays no role in choosing the president.

items.prompt: A president vetoes a bill passed by Congress, and Congress considers overriding the veto. Which constitutional principle is most directly illustrated?
choices: Popular sovereignty without representation
Checks and balances
The supremacy of state constitutions
Direct democracy in the national legislature
items.rationale: Checks and balances allow each branch to restrain actions by another branch, while the veto and override process also reflects separation of powers.
choiceRationales: A veto and override are actions by elected branches checking each other, not the people acting without representatives.
Checks and balances allow each branch to restrain actions by another branch, while the veto and override process also reflects separation of powers.
The scenario involves only national institutions; state constitutions are not in play, and federal law is supreme over them anyway.
Congress is a representative body; an override vote by members is a check on the executive, not direct citizen lawmaking.

items.prompt: A state law conflicts with a valid federal law enacted under constitutional authority. Which principle generally resolves the conflict?
choices: The Tenth Amendment routinely invalidates any federal statute affecting a state.
The Senate decides which state laws are constitutional without judicial review.
The Supremacy Clause gives lawful federal statutes priority over state law.
State law generally prevails because states predated the federal government.
items.rationale: The Supremacy Clause establishes that the Constitution, valid federal laws, and treaties take priority over conflicting state law.
choiceRationales: The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the states; it does not cancel valid federal laws that touch state interests.
Constitutional conflicts between state and federal law are resolved in courts under the Supremacy Clause, not by a Senate vote.
The Supremacy Clause establishes that the Constitution, valid federal laws, and treaties take priority over conflicting state law.
Article VI’s Supremacy Clause establishes that the Constitution and valid federal statutes take precedence over conflicting state laws regardless of whether the states existed prior to ratification.

items.prompt: Which constitutional interpretation did McCulloch v. Maryland support?
choices: Congress is limited to powers listed word-for-word in Article I, leaving implied powers outside its scope.
States may tax or veto any federal institution that operates within their borders whenever they object to it.
The Supreme Court reviews state criminal disputes while leaving federal constitutional questions to Congress.
Congress holds implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause, and states cannot block federal actions.
items.rationale: McCulloch supported implied congressional powers and national supremacy by rejecting Maryland’s attempt to tax the national bank.
choiceRationales: McCulloch rejected this strict reading, holding that the Necessary and Proper Clause supports implied powers such as chartering a bank.
The Court held the opposite: Maryland could not tax the national bank because the power to tax is the power to destroy.
McCulloch was a civil case about a bank tax; it says nothing limiting the Court to criminal matters.
McCulloch supported implied congressional powers and national supremacy by rejecting Maryland’s attempt to tax the national bank.

items.learningObjectiveLabel: Explain and apply topic 1.8: constitutional interpretations of federalism in a constitutional, institutional, or civic context.

items.prompt: Why can federalism create multiple access points for an interest group seeking a policy change?
choices: Advocates can pursue policy change through both national institutions and state governments.
Federalism requires every policy change to be approved separately by every level of government before it takes effect.
Federalism removes state governments from policy implementation and leaves national agencies as the only venue.
Federalism gives courts exclusive control over public policy, so advocacy outside litigation cannot succeed.
items.rationale: Shared authority creates more than one venue for advocacy, implementation, litigation, and coalition building.
choiceRationales: Shared authority creates more than one venue for advocacy, implementation, litigation, and coalition building.
Levels of government act within their own authority; a policy does not need approval from all of them, which is what creates alternative venues.
States carry out much national policy and make their own; that shared role is why groups can lobby at either level.
Courts resolve disputes; legislatures and executives at both levels make and implement policy, and groups can approach any of them.

items.prompt: Which statement best connects the Declaration of Independence to the principle of popular sovereignty?
choices: It establishes a lifetime national judiciary with power to veto legislation.
It roots legitimate authority in the consent and rights of the people.
It gives Congress exclusive authority over local elections.
It argues that political authority should be inherited through monarchy.
items.rationale: The Declaration frames legitimate government as grounded in the rights and consent of the governed, a foundation for popular sovereignty.
choiceRationales: The Declaration creates no institutions; the judiciary comes from Article III of the Constitution, and courts do not veto bills.
The Declaration frames legitimate government as grounded in the rights and consent of the governed, a foundation for popular sovereignty.
The Declaration does not assign powers to Congress, and election administration is largely a state responsibility.

The Declaration of Independence explicitly rejected hereditary monarchy and divine right, arguing instead that legitimate political authority derives from natural rights and the consent of the governed.

A national government with separated powers would automatically abolish the states.
A distant national government could threaten individual liberty and state authority.
items.rationale: Brutus argued that a large, centralized republic could become unresponsive and endanger liberty, a core Anti-Federalist concern.
choiceRationales: Brutus feared a strong, distant national government, not a weak one, and local elections were never the concern.
That is closer to Madison’s argument in reverse; Brutus favored small republics as more accountable to citizens.
Brutus worried states would be gradually overshadowed by national power, not automatically abolished by separation of powers.
Brutus argued that a large, centralized republic could become unresponsive and endanger liberty, a core Anti-Federalist concern.

items.prompt: Which weakness of the Articles of Confederation most directly limited Congress’s ability to pay national debts?

Congress controlled a permanent national executive with unlimited funds.
Congress had exclusive control over all state courts.
Congress could regulate every interstate trade dispute without limitation.
items.rationale: The Confederation Congress depended on state contributions and lacked a general direct taxing power, limiting its fiscal capacity.
choiceRationales: The Confederation Congress depended on state contributions and lacked a general direct taxing power, limiting its fiscal capacity.
The Articles created no national executive and gave Congress no independent revenue, which is why debts went unpaid.
State courts remained under state control; the Confederation had no authority over them and no national judiciary.

Congress possessed no commerce authority under the Articles of Confederation, leaving interstate trade disputes unresolved while its separate inability to levy taxes prevented reliable repayment of national debts.

items.prompt: Why did the promise to add a Bill of Rights help some Anti-Federalists accept ratification?

It eased fears that national power could threaten personal liberties.
It transferred all federal powers to state legislatures.
It guaranteed that the president would be selected by direct popular vote.

The Bill of Rights responded to concerns that constitutional limits and structural checks alone might not adequately protect individual liberties.
The amendments limit national power in specific ways; they do not hand federal powers to the states.

Adding the Bill of Rights left the Electoral College system intact and did not create a direct popular presidential vote; it instead addressed Anti-Federalist concerns by placing explicit limits on federal power.

items.prompt: Which power is generally reserved to the states by the federal system?
choices: Coining national currency and setting the value of money used throughout the United States
Negotiating treaties with foreign governments and appointing ambassadors to represent the nation
Declaring war on another country and raising the armed forces that would conduct it
Administering local elections and public schools within constitutional limits
items.rationale: State and local governments retain many powers over education and election administration, while currency, treaties, and war are national powers.
choiceRationales: Coining money is an enumerated national power in Article I, and states are expressly barred from it.

Article II assigns treaty negotiation and ambassadorial appointments to the president with Senate advice and consent, while Article I, Section 10 expressly prohibits states from entering into foreign treaties.

Article I, Section 8 vests the authority to declare war and raise and support armed forces exclusively in Congress, making national defense a federal enumerated power rather than a reserved state power.
State and local governments retain many powers over education and election administration, while currency, treaties, and war are national powers.

items.prompt: A case asks whether Congress may regulate an activity that affects interstate markets only indirectly. Which constitutional authority is most likely at issue?
choices: The Commerce Clause
The Appointments Clause
The Treaty Clause
The Establishment Clause
items.rationale: The Commerce Clause is the principal constitutional basis for disputes over the federal regulation of interstate economic activity.
choiceRationales: The Commerce Clause is the principal constitutional basis for disputes over the federal regulation of interstate economic activity.
The Appointments Clause in Article II governs how the president nominates and the Senate confirms federal officers and judges, and it provides no authority for Congress to regulate economic markets.

The Treaty Clause governs formal international agreements negotiated by the president and approved by two-thirds of the Senate, rather than domestic congressional regulation of commercial activity across state lines.

The Establishment Clause of the First Amendment restricts government endorsement or sponsorship of religion, so it has no bearing on whether Congress may regulate activities connected to interstate markets.

items.prompt: Which presidential role is most directly illustrated when the president negotiates with a foreign government on behalf of the United States?
choices: Chief legislator of every state
Chief diplomat
Chief justice of the Supreme Court
Speaker of the House
items.rationale: The president acts as chief diplomat when conducting foreign relations, although treaties require Senate approval.

Testing campaign appeals and refining voter outreach are tools for persuading citizens to cast ballots in competitive elections, not a mechanism for appointing judges.
Tracking audience feedback to adjust outreach actively strengthens supporter mobilization and routinely works alongside party infrastructure rather than abolishing political parties.
Federalism distributes constitutional governing powers between national and state governments; it does not describe a campaign using data analytics to tailor voter communications.

items.prompt: A campaign-finance rule requires an organization to disclose its donors and spending for an advertisement. What democratic concern does disclosure address?
choices: Disclosure guarantees that every political claim in an advertisement is entirely true.
Helping voters judge which interests and funds back political speech
Disclosure prevents all organizations from speaking about matters of public policy.
Disclosure transfers all election administration to the United States Supreme Court.
items.rationale: Disclosure gives voters information about who funds political communication, although it does not itself establish the truth of every message.
choiceRationales: Campaign-finance reporting identifies the donors and committees paying for political speech so citizens can judge potential bias, but it does not certify the factual accuracy of claims.
Disclosure gives voters information about who funds political communication, although it does not itself establish the truth of every message.
Transparency rules require groups to publish funding sources while leaving them free to run issue ads and political commentary under First Amendment protections.
State and local election officials continue running voting and ballot administration; campaign-finance transparency laws do not shift electoral operations to the federal judiciary.

items.prompt: A news outlet gives repeated attention to housing costs, leading candidates to discuss the issue more often. Which media effect is most directly suggested?
choices: Prior restraint requires the government to select which issues the outlet may cover.
Judicial review means that the outlet can invalidate any housing legislation it dislikes.
Agenda setting by raising a topic’s prominence in public debate
Cloture ends every public discussion as soon as the outlet publishes a single story.
items.rationale: Agenda setting concerns the issues that receive attention and become more salient, not necessarily the specific opinion citizens adopt.
choiceRationales: Prior restraint refers to unconstitutional government censorship blocking publication in advance, whereas here an independent newsroom voluntarily prioritized housing-cost reporting.
Only federal and state courts exercise judicial review to strike down unconstitutional statutes; journalists influence public debate without holding legal power to void laws.
Agenda setting concerns the issues that receive attention and become more salient, not necessarily the specific opinion citizens adopt.
Cloture is a procedural Senate vote requiring 60 senators to close floor debate on a measure and bears no connection to how news coverage elevates campaign topics.

items.learningObjectiveLabel: Explain and apply topic 5.12: the media in a constitutional, institutional, or civic context.

items.prompt: Citizens receive political news through many personalized feeds and disagree about which facts deserve attention. What tradeoff is most relevant?
choices: A greater number of media choices guarantees that all citizens receive entirely identical information each day.
Personalized news feeds eliminate every possibility of political participation by ordinary citizens at all.
Media fragmentation means that all of the political claims that citizens encounter are equally reliable.
Fragmented feeds widen choice while reinforcing selective exposure and factual divides.
items.rationale: Changing media environments can expand access and participation while encouraging selective exposure, polarization, uneven knowledge, and weaker shared agendas.
choiceRationales: Expanding cable channels, podcasts, and personalized feeds splinters audiences across divergent sources, reducing shared news exposure rather than delivering identical daily information.
People participate through and alongside personalized feeds; feeds change information flows, not the ability to act.
A proliferation of outlets mixes vetted journalism with partisan commentary and unverified rumors, requiring citizens to evaluate source credibility rather than assuming equal reliability.
Changing media environments can expand access and participation while encouraging selective exposure, polarization, uneven knowledge, and weaker shared agendas.

bigIdeas.label: Constitutionalism
bigIdeas.description: The Constitution establishes a system of checks, balances, and limits on government power.

bigIdeas.label: Liberty and Order
bigIdeas.description: Political institutions and citizens continually negotiate the relationship between individual liberty and public order.

bigIdeas.label: Civic Participation in a Representative Democracy
bigIdeas.description: Citizens and organized groups use multiple pathways to influence representation and policy.

bigIdeas.label: Competing Policymaking Interests
bigIdeas.description: Institutions, parties, interests, and citizens compete and cooperate to shape public policy.

bigIdeas.label: Methods of Political Analysis
bigIdeas.description: Political scientists use concepts, cases, data, sources, and arguments to analyze government and politics.

skills.label: Concept Application
skills.description: Describe, compare, and apply political principles, institutions, processes, policies, and behaviors.

skills.label: SCOTUS Application
skills.description: Apply required Supreme Court case facts, holdings, reasoning, and constitutional connections.

skills.label: Data Analysis
skills.description: Describe, interpret, compare, and evaluate quantitative and visual political data.

skills.label: Source Analysis
skills.description: Read, analyze, and interpret foundational documents and other text-based or visual sources.

skills.label: Argumentation
skills.description: Make defensible claims, support them with evidence and reasoning, and address alternatives.
